content: The impact of psychological interventions on inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains a topic of debate. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of psychological therapies, including psychotherapy, patient education, and relaxation techniques, on health-related quality of life, coping mechanisms, emotional well-being, and disease activity in individuals with IBD. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including Medline, Embase, LILACS, Psyndex, CINAHL, PsyInfo, CCMed, SOMED, and Social SciSearch, covering studies from their inception to April 2010. Conference abstracts and reference lists were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria required randomized, quasi-randomized, or non-randomized controlled trials involving children or adults with IBD, with a minimum follow-up period of two months. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Statistical analyses were conducted using a random-effects model to calculate pooled standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 21 studies, involving 1,745 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 19 studies focused on adults, while 2 studies involved adolescents. Most studies employed multimodal approaches. However, the overall risk of bias was high across all studies. In adults, psychotherapy did not demonstrate any significant effect on quality of life at approximately 12 months (3 studies, 235 patients; SMD -0.07; 95% CI -0.33 to 0.19). Similarly, there was no significant impact on emotional status, specifically depression (4 studies, 266 patients; SMD 0.03; 95% CI -0.22 to 0.27), or on the proportion of patients not in remission (5 studies, 287 patients; OR 0.85; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.48). Comparable results were observed at 3 to 8 months of follow-up. There was no evidence of statistical heterogeneity or subgroup effects based on the type of IBD or the intensity of the psychological therapy. In adolescents, psychotherapy showed positive short-term effects on several outcomes, including quality of life (2 studies, 71 patients; SMD 0.70; 95% CI 0.21 to 1.18) and depression (1 study, 41 patients; SMD -0.62; 95% CI -1.25 to 0.01). However, these findings were limited to short-term follow-up periods. Educational interventions did not yield significant improvements in quality of life at 12 months (5 studies, 947 patients; SMD 0.11; 95% CI -0.02 to 0.24), depression (3 studies, 378 patients; SMD -0.08; 95% CI -0.29 to 0.12), or the proportion of patients not in remission (3 studies, 434 patients; OR 1.00; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.53). Importantly, no adverse events were reported in any of the included studies. In conclusion, there is no robust evidence to support the efficacy of psychological therapies in improving outcomes for adult patients with IBD. In adolescents, psychological interventions may offer some benefits, but the evidence is limited and primarily short-term. Further research is necessary to determine the effectiveness of these therapies in specific subgroups of patients who may require psychological support and to identify the most effective types of psychological interventions for these populations.
